content.title: Diesel vs Gas: Everything You Need to Know
content.text: The fuel price signs at interstate exits deliver a simple message about diesel vs. gas: Diesel typically is more expensive than gas. While it’s true diesel fuel generally costs more than regular and mid-grade gas — not premium, though, and not 100 percent of the time or everywhere — but that’s only part of the story.Although diesel-powered engines have become more common in the United States in recent years, they still trail gas engines by a wide margin. Overseas, higher gas prices and tax incentives make diesels more economical choices, but even in Europe, for example, diesel sales have been decreasing since the introduction of stricter emissions standards in the 2010s — not to mention the rise of electric and hybrid vehicles.Today, if you want a diesel vehicle in the United States, you’ll be looking at pickup trucks, full-size SUVs, or larger vans: Chevrolet Express 2500/3500 cargo van; Chevrolet Silverado 1500/2500/3500; Chevrolet Suburban; Chevrolet Tahoe; Ford F-250 SD/F-350 SD/F-450 SD; GMC Sierra 1500/2500 HD/3500 HD; GMC Yukon; Mercedes Sprinter cargo and crew vans; Ram 2500/3500; Ram ProMaster cargo van 1500/2500; and Ram ProMaster 2500 window van.A Brief History of Diesel in the United StatesOver the past 40 years, automakers have introduced diesel engines in the United States, but they are much rarer, found exclusively in pickup trucks and a handful of SUVs. Relatively low gas prices have stunted demand for more fuel-efficient engines. More recently, hybrid gas-electric and electric-only powertrains have pushed diesels further aside. And lest we forget, Volkswagen cheated on diesel emissions tests in 2015, leading Volkswagen, Audi, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, and other brands to pull most diesels from the U.S. market.Still, diesel engines have a loyal following, particularly among those who tow heavy boats and trailers and other cargo. That’s why they remain popular in pickup trucks.Credit: Getty ImagesDiesel vs. Gas: The DifferencesMost people equate gas with passenger vehicles and diesel with big rigs and work trucks. That’s not totally accurate, but the perception is rooted in reality.Let’s start with an origin story: Gas and diesel are petroleum products refined from crude oil. Diesel is easier to refine; gas is more refined. The additional refinement makes gas thinner and more volatile while diesel is thicker. This difference in density means a lot in practical terms. Gas burns faster, enabling it to produce more horsepower. Diesel, on the other hand, burns slowly. The result: Diesel creates 20% more energy than gasoline engines using the same amount of fuel. Gas and diesel engines use a four-stroke internal combustion cycle to power vehicles, converting fuel to energy: intake, compression, power, and exhaust. In simple terms, the engine burns a mixture of fuel and air in a confined space (the combustion chamber or cylinder), creating a rapid expansion of hot gases that pushes a piston, which in turn rotates a crankshaft, converting linear motion into rotational motion that powers the vehicle's wheels.Where gas and diesel engines differ is in the combustion process.Combustion in gas engines: The fuel is first mixed with air, then compressed by the piston. Next, a spark plug ignites the fuel to cause the explosion that moves the piston that moves the wheels.Combustion in diesel engines: Since diesels do not have spark plugs, diesel-engine combustion uses extreme compression to create the heat needed for ignition — aka compression ignition. Only air is drawn into the cylinder (combustion chamber) and highly compressed during the compression stroke. At the peak of compression, the diesel fuel is injected into the superheated compressed air. The extremely high temperature of the compressed air causes the diesel fuel to spontaneously ignite (autoignition) without the need for a spark.Diesel vs. Gas Compression RatiosCompression ratio is how much an engine compresses the air inside before burning fuel.Gas engines: Compress less (around 8 to 12 times). As gas engines mix fuel with air, too much compression makes the fuel explode too early (engine knock). A spark plug starts the controlled burn.Diesel engines: Compress around 14 to 25 times. Diesels only compress air, making it extremely hot. Then, fuel is sprayed into this super-hot air, and it ignites instantly from the heat.Compression ratio directly impacts an engine's power output, fuel economy, and overall durability. Credit: Getty ImagesHow Diesel and Gas CompareFor many Americans, their knowledge of diesel vs. gas begins and ends with the price per gallon for each. But the fuels have many differences that buyers should keep in mind when considering a new vehicle.Efficiency and CostAll that talk about fuel density and compression ratios earlier is about to translate to bottom-line economics.Fuel efficiency: Diesel-powered vehicles are generally the more fuel efficient of the two. This is true for several reasons:Remember, diesel is 20% more efficient than gas thanks to its higher density, which allows it to generate more energy with less fuel. Diesel engines can operate at a lower RPM while producing the same amount of power.Since diesel engines operate at higher compression ratios, they have better thermal efficiency, which improves fuel efficiency. Higher compression ratios produce more energy. Gas, on the other hand, cannot operate at those high ratios because it ignites at lower temperatures.Upfront costs: Diesels are more expensive than gas engines, sometimes by knee-buckling amounts. On the Ford F-250 Super Duty, for example, a version with the 6.7-liter turbodiesel engine costs $11,000 more than one with the standard gas V8. On the Ram 2500 Laramie, a 6.7-liter turbodiesel Cummins engine adds $12,500 to the bottom line.Diesel can also be more expensive and harder to find. If you’re on the interstate, you’ll have no problem, but not every station in the suburbs or a downtown metro area will have it because diesel requires a separate underground tank and a separate pump. Plus, refueling with diesel at some stations can require fueling next to 18-wheelers or other large trucks. That can be an unpleasant experience.Overall cost of ownership: In the long run, the higher fuel costs and higher maintenance costs, plus the higher initial purchase price, might make a diesel too costly for some consumers. While gas consumes more fuel, needs more frequent maintenance, and might need more care as mileage piles up after 100,000 miles, all those cost less than their diesel counterparts. Ford F-150 / Photo Credit: FordPerformance and PowerMore torque for towing: For many who tow, a diesel is often the preferred option because it produces more torque — the power needed to pull heavy loads, such as large boats, horse trailers, and other vehicles. Diesel engines produce large amounts of torque at low speeds and across a broad range of engine speeds, making them well-suited for towing. They typically have a greater towing capacity than gas engines.For example, the Ford F-250 (with single rear wheels) can tow up to 14,800 pounds with a gas V8 engine, but can tow 20,000 pounds with the 6.7-liter turbodiesel V8.The Ram 2500 can tow up to 20,000 pounds with its 6.7-liter diesel engine, about 2,000 pounds more than the 6.4-liter V8. The difference is in the diesel’s massive amount of torque, 1,079 pound-feet, compared to 429. Not as useful in sporty cars: There’s a reason you don’t see diesel engines in many sports cars — diesel motors can’t match the performance of gas motors when you want a lightweight, high-revving, high-horsepower engine.Because diesel engines have heavier blocks, lower RPM redlines, and favor torque for towing over horsepower for high-speed acceleration, they’re better in trucks than performance vehicles.Ram 2500 Heavy Duty Rebel / Credit: StellantisDurability and LifespanDiesel engines typically last longer than gas engines, especially under grueling towing conditions, because diesels are usually built with stronger parts designed to withstand sustained hard use. For this reason, diesel engines are often the preferred choice of fleet operators, such as delivery services and utilities. Those companies want to keep vehicles in service as long as they can — 300,000 miles or more — to reduce costs, and diesels are often regarded as a better long-term bet than gas engines.MaintenanceIn most cases, diesel engines have larger oil capacities than gas engines and may require more expensive types of oil. For example, a Ford 6.2-liter gas V8 engine requires 7 quarts of oil, whereas its 6.7-liter diesel engine requires 15 quarts. So that $29.99 oil change you see advertised probably won’t apply to a diesel pickup. When something breaks on a diesel engine, it’s likely to cost more to replace than on a gas engine because diesels use heavier-duty parts and have more elaborate and specialized emissions controls to reduce particulate emissions. One piece of good news here: Diesel engines have fewer components than gas engines, so you have fewer chances of something going wrong.Another thing to consider: Not every mechanic has the tools or training to work on diesels, so there may be fewer options for who can do the work, which can drive up the cost.EmissionsModern diesel engines produce fewer pollutants thanks to better emissions systems and diesel fuel with lower sulfur content. Companies that make diesel vehicles and diesel fuel capitalized on those advances by touting their products as “clean diesel.”Diesel engines in cars and light trucks must meet the exact emissions requirements as gas engines. Some scientific studies have shown that current diesels are as clean or cleaner than gas engines, except for the amount of nitrogen oxides they produce. Nitrogen oxides, or NOx, cause smog.Credit: Getty ImagesWhat Fuel is Right For You?This decision ultimately comes down to the type of driver you are and the type of vehicle you want to drive. First, if you opt for a diesel vehicle, you’ll have to settle for a limited selection of pickups and vans, as no passenger vehicles are currently available with a diesel engine.If you drive a lot and often tow or haul large loads, the power of a diesel engine is ideal, and the costs are justifiable over the long term. Higher fuel economy and the longevity of diesel engines can even out the initial sticker shock and higher maintenance costs, especially in diesel vans and heavy-duty trucks.For most daily, regular-use drivers, a gas-fueled vehicle is suitable and is more economical. With a lower off-the-lot price, lower maintenance costs, and lower fuel prices, gas is easier on the bottom line.Next StepsCheck out new and used cars for saleBuy a Carfax Vehicle History ReportResearch your next vehicle
